newsitem.title: NORWAY: Holbrooke, Clinton tipped for Nobel Peace Prize.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke, Clinton tipped for Nobel Peace Prize.

text.p: Norway's secretive Nobel Committee will gather next week for what may be the final decision on the choice for the 1996 Peace Prize, with Bosnian mediator Richard Holbrooke and President Bill Clinton among the front-runners.
The five-member committee will meet in Oslo on October 2, just over a week before the prestigious award is due to be announced at 11 a.m. local time (0900 GMT) on October 11.
Geir Lundestad, Director of the Nobel Institute, said another meeting had been tentatively penned for October 8 in case the committee found itself in deadlock.
"No final decision has been made yet, we may need an additional meeting if the winner is undecided next week. We like to keep the decision open for as long as possible," Lundestad told Reuters.
One hundred and twenty candidates, including 29 organisations, were nominated for the 1996 award, many repeated from last year's nominees, he said.
The deadline for nominations was January 31, but any application stamped before that date would be included on the list.

The Norwegian news agency NTB said on Tuesday U.S. peace mediator in Bosnia Holbrooke was favourite for the award, although he may have to share the million dollar prize money with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Bosnia held its first post-war election this month, a central plank in the implementation of the 1995 Dayton treaty which Holbrooke almost single-handedly negotiated as assistant U.S. secretary of state after years of hapless U.N. and European mediation.
Lundestad emphasised that Holbrooke's recent visit to the Nobel Foundation as guest speaker to the Norwegian Atlantic Committee was not linked to the prize, NTB said.

NTB said the 1996 list included several former nominees such as Chinese dissident Wei Jingsheng, former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, jailed Kurdish politician Leyla Zana and jailed Israeli nuclear technician Mordechai Vanunu.

Others under consideration were Catholic bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo for his role in the fight for recognition of Indonesian-ruled East Timor as a state, Mexican bishop Samuel Ruiz, who mediated between the Mexican government and the rebel Chiapas Indians, and Cambodian monk Maha Ghosandnada, known as the "Gandhi of Cambodia", for his efforts to reconcile the country after the overthrow of the Khmer Rouge in 1979.
Organisations to be renominated included The Salvation Army and medical charity Medicins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders), the agency added.
A shortlist of candidates was drawn up at the end of February.
The selection process surrounding peace award is shrouded in secrecy and the Norwegian Nobel Committee refuses to reveal the shortlist nor even the names of nominees.
The 1995 peace laureates were veteran anti-nuclear campaigner Joseph Rotblat and his Pugwash organisation.
